title: Executive orders: authority, operation, and enforceability
shortTitle: Executive orders: authority, operation, and enforceability
summary: An executive order is a formal presidential directive whose legal effect depends on constitutional or statutory authority and the specific obligation it creates.
notes:
Executive orders communicate presidential commands in a formal written instrument; memoranda and proclamations may perform similar functions. The reading describes consultation through OMB and the Justice Department, presidential signature, and publication under the Federal Register framework. The label on the document does not establish its legal force. Youngstown requires a source of constitutional or statutory authority.

Some orders allocate work, coordinate agencies, direct study, or announce regulatory priorities within the executive branch. Others exercise authority delegated by statute and may affect the public directly. Procurement examples illustrate both the potential breadth of statutory authority and judicial limits when an order conflicts with other laws. An instruction to use discretion to the extent permitted by law preserves the statutory boundary; it does not repeal an underlying enactment. Orders also participate in interbranch bargaining by preserving resources while Congress considers legislation or by initiating permissible action when legislation stalls.

A person who benefits from an order does not automatically obtain a private right to enforce it. The excerpt describes explicit disclaimers of judicial enforceability and decisions finding insufficient presidential authority to create privately enforceable obligations without congressional authorization. Nor does an order directed at an agency automatically replace the agency’s own statutory decision process. The historical examples run through the administrations addressed in the textbook; they are not a current inventory of orders in force.
